title: Under‐Ice Thermal and Oxygen Dynamics in Brackish Lakes on the Tibetan Plateau
content:
Abstract

Under-ice circulation in freshwater lakes is predominantly governed by thermal regimes. In contrast, saline alpine lakes, particularly those on the Tibetan Plateau (TP), are expected to exhibit hydrodynamics where solute redistribution, not temperature alone, dictates density stratification and dissolved oxygen (DO) transport. This study synthesizes high-frequency in situ mooring observations from three brackish TP lakes covering a wide salinity range (Nam Co, 1.51 ± 0.01 g L−1; Selin Co, 11.42 ± 0.04 g L−1; and Bamu Co, 12.16 ± 0.05 g L−1), to quantify how salinity gradients reshape under-ice physics and DO regimes. The results showed that: (a) In Nam Co, although under-ice benthic salinity accumulation sustains surface-bottom density differences, it facilitated the transport of oxygenated water to the bottom; (b) In more saline Selin Co and Bamu Co, chemical gradients were found to contribute more than thermal gradients to under-ice total water column stability (Schmidt stability, St); (c) Compared to low-salinity Nam Co, high salinity lowers the temperature of maximum density (T md) to 1.20°C in Bamu Co and 1.36°C in Selin Co, respectively. This allows positive thermal stratification (warmer at the surface, colder at depth) to begin roughly 2 weeks before ice-off; and (d) This combined thermal-chemical stratification suppresses spring turnover, delaying benthic ventilation of DO by nearly 1 month after ice-off. These findings underscore the important role of chemical gradients in under-ice dynamics in saline lakes, with critical implications for predicting limnological responses to climate-driven lake desalination and ice-loss across high-altitude cryospheric regions on the TP.
